clue.text: Winged fruit — often seeded one seen over weekend. Yes?

indicators.note: the tennis player's name is laid over the letter for the weekend, wrapping round it

parts.note: Arthur Ashe, the American tennis champion, was often a seeded player in tournaments
the end of the word week is K

explanation.surface: A botanical note on a seeded fruit, oddly mixed with a weekend sighting and a hopeful question.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Seeded' suggests plants, but it means a ranked tennis player: Arthur ASHE. 'Seen over' puts ASHE round K, the end of 'week', giving ASHKE; add Y for 'Yes'.
explanation.definitionFit: The winged seed pods of the ash tree hang in bunches called keys.

clue.text: Cow longing to stand under tree

indicators.note: in a down answer the second piece sits below the tree

parts.note: an alder is a tree of damp ground

indicators.note: in a down clue, standing up means the word longing is read from the bottom upwards

parts.note: a yen is a longing

explanation.surface: A cow is pining to stand in the shade of a tree.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To stand' turns YEN upwards to NEY, placed under ALDER.
explanation.definitionFit: An Alderney is a breed of dairy cattle from the Channel Island of that name.

clue.text: Exercise for judges and journalists

parts.note: the bench is the collective term for judges or magistrates
the press means journalists collectively

explanation.surface: A suggested workout routine for the legal and newspaper professions.
explanation.definitionFit: A weightlifting move done lying on a bench and pushing a barbell upwards.

clue.text: Proceed with difficulty, lacking (5,5) resilience

explanation.surface: Someone struggles onward, worn out and without any bounce left.
explanation.walkthrough: The '(5,5)' inside the clue is a stray from the printed page and plays no part.
explanation.definitionFit: To hobble along is to walk lamely; floppy, without firmness or spring, is the other sense.

clue.text: Foul cast — or cast keeping in the White shade?

indicators.note: to cast metal is to remould it, so the letters are reshaped into a new order

explanation.surface: A theatrical complaint: a poor cast, or a cast that keeps a white-faced pallor?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cast' appears twice: the first is fodder, the second is the anagram signal working on FOUL CAST OR.
explanation.definitionFit: Fabric that is dye-fast holds its hue, keeping the same shade wash after wash.

clue.text: Sad expression of a girl falling short

indicators.note: falling short means the word for girl stops before its final letter

parts.note: a lass is a girl

explanation.surface: A sigh of sadness as a girl fails to reach her goal.
explanation.definitionFit: An exclamation of grief or regret, an interjection voicing sorrow.

clue.text: Modest objection to drug

parts.note: a demur is an objection or hesitation
E is short for the drug ecstasy

explanation.surface: A mild protest against taking drugs.
explanation.definitionFit: Shy and reserved in manner, a synonym for modest.

clue.text: Upper part of letter or card seen when it's sorted

indicators.note: sorting puts things into a fresh order, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Something in the mail, perhaps a card, revealed once the post is sorted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sorted' rearranges CARD SEEN.
explanation.definitionFit: In typography, the stroke of a lowercase letter such as b or d rising above the x-height.

clue.text: Game in which France and Ireland battle

indicators.note: the card game holds the other two pieces inside it

parts.note: solo is a card game, solo whist
F is the international vehicle code for France
Erin is a poetic name for Ireland

explanation.surface: A rugby match where France and Ireland clash.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Game' and 'battle' both suggest the sports field. Solferino (1859) was a battle in northern Italy.
explanation.definitionFit: Solferino was the 1859 clash of French and Austrian armies whose carnage inspired the Red Cross.

clue.text: City guides announced

indicators.note: announced means the word for guides is spoken, giving a sound-alike

parts.note: to guide is to lead, so guides are leads

explanation.surface: Tour guides in a city are introduced to the group.
explanation.definitionFit: A large city in Yorkshire in northern England.

clue.text: A bone can keep fracturing

indicators.note: fracturing breaks the words up so the letters re-form in a new order

explanation.surface: A bone can stay broken.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fracturing' rearranges CAN KEEP; 'A bone' is the definition, not part of the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: The patella, the small flat bone covering the front of the knee joint.

clue.text: Bob's not the first with remedy Jude 5 21 was

indicators.note: the opening letter of the word is dropped

parts.note: taken as the letters of the word
a cure is a remedy

explanation.surface: A man named Bob plays second fiddle with a cure, like a figure from Hardy.
explanation.walkthrough: Thomas Hardy's novel is 'Jude the Obscure', so Jude was obscure; '5 21' is a scanning slip on the page, probably for 'as'.
explanation.definitionFit: Hardy's title calls his hero Jude unknown and humble, the meaning of the word here.

clue.text: That is the result when UK abandons Canadian territory

indicators.note: abandons means the letters UK leave the name of the territory

parts.note: the Yukon is a territory of north-west Canada

explanation.surface: Britain withdrawing from a northern Canadian territory, with a stated outcome.
explanation.walkthrough: YON is an old word for 'that' (as in 'yon hill').
explanation.definitionFit: An old or dialect demonstrative meaning that one over there.

clue.text: Safe leisure centre attended by all runners in Hampshire

parts.note: peter is old criminal slang for a safe

indicators.note: the centre of a word is its middle letter

parts.note: the field is all the runners in a race

explanation.surface: A secure leisure centre with every runner in a southern county attending.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Peter' for a safe is safecrackers' slang. Petersfield is a market town in Hampshire, a county on England's south coast.
explanation.definitionFit: Petersfield is a market town found in that southern English county.

clue.text: Running cotton mills, taking time off for a cocktail

indicators.note: running a mill makes it work differently, so the letters are rearranged
taking it off means one letter of the fodder is removed
off completes the instruction to drop the letter for time from the fodder

explanation.surface: Managing textile factories, then knocking off for a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Taking time off' removes one T from COTTON MILLS; 'Running' rearranges the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: A gin, lemon juice, sugar and soda drink served in a tall glass.

clue.text: Cosmetic support for the establishment?

explanation.surface: A make-up base described as propping up the ruling class.
explanation.definitionFit: Make-up base applied under other cosmetics; also the setting up of an institution, or the institution itself.

clue.text: Man of law-or young man on fringes of legislature

parts.note: a boy is a young man

indicators.note: the fringes of a word are its first and last letters

explanation.surface: A lawman, or a youth hanging around the edges of parliament.
explanation.walkthrough: Robert Boyle gave his name to Boyle's law of gases, hence 'Man of law'.
explanation.definitionFit: The scientist Robert Boyle is known for the gas law named after him.

clue.text: Look for shopkeepers with mince heart?

explanation.surface: Searching for meat sellers who chop up hearts.
explanation.walkthrough: Butcher's hook is Cockney rhyming slang for 'look', shortened to 'butcher's' (as in 'have a butcher's').
explanation.definitionFit: A glance, from rhyming slang; also meat traders who grind up offal such as hearts.

clue.text: Big bird initially discovered by Margaret of Anjou

indicators.note: initially takes the first letter of each of the following words

explanation.surface: A large bird found by a medieval queen.
explanation.walkthrough: Margaret of Anjou was the queen of Henry VI.
explanation.definitionFit: An extinct giant flightless bird of New Zealand.

clue.text: Without reservation, so to speak

explanation.surface: Speaking freely and holding nothing back.
explanation.definitionFit: Complete or absolute is one meaning; to say or voice words is the verb sense.

clue.text: Road where fish may be seen on cycle?

indicators.note: in a down answer the fish sits on top of, after, the cycle

parts.note: a turn is a cycle or rotation
a pike is a fish

explanation.surface: A road where a fish might be spotted riding a bicycle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cycle' suggests a bicycle, but it means a turn or rotation.
explanation.definitionFit: A toll road, especially a highway in the US.

clue.text: Ecstatic, as convicts were

explanation.surface: Thrilled, like prisoners sent off to Australia.
explanation.walkthrough: British convicts were sentenced to transportation to penal colonies such as Australia.
explanation.definitionFit: Carried away with joy; also shipped overseas as punishment.

clue.text: Like mid-Atlantic listing

parts.note: as means like

indicators.note: mid- takes the middle of the word, dropping letters at each end

explanation.surface: A ship heeling over in the middle of the ocean.
explanation.walkthrough: The middle of ATLANTIC is LANT, with AT and IC removed from the ends.
explanation.definitionFit: Leaning at an angle, as a ship heels over.

clue.text: Curious spirit

explanation.surface: An odd alcoholic drink.
explanation.definitionFit: Odd or strange in old slang; also the spirit distilled from sugar cane.

clue.text: Children of Benjamin or Simeon

indicators.note: of means the letters are taken out of the names that follow

explanation.surface: The sons of two of the patriarch Jacob's sons in the Bible.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer runs across the end of 'Benjamin', the word 'or' and the start of 'Simeon'.
explanation.definitionFit: Legally, people under the age of adulthood.

clue.text: Only one item of luggage required?

definitions.text: Only one item of luggage required?

parts.words: Only one item of luggage required?
parts.note: read as a single bag big enough to carry every possession, so nothing else need be packed

explanation.surface: A traveller asking whether they really need just one bag.
explanation.definitionFit: A large bag for carrying everything when travelling.

clue.text: Primate holding service primarily in would church recess

indicators.note: the primate's word holds the letter inside it

parts.note: an ape is a primate

indicators.note: primarily takes the first letter of the word

explanation.surface: An archbishop holding a service in a recess of the church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Primate' suggests an archbishop in this church setting, but it is the ape.
explanation.definitionFit: A semicircular vaulted recess at the east end of a church.

clue.text: Sort of job one almost has taken advantage of

parts.note: a put-up job is a set-up or fraud

indicators.note: almost means the word stops short of its last letter

explanation.surface: Somebody who has almost got a fraudulent job and is exploited.
explanation.definitionFit: Exploited or imposed upon by others.

clue.text: A short break, we hear, for the hands

indicators.note: we hear means the phrase for a short break is spoken, giving a sound-alike

parts.note: a pause is a short break

explanation.surface: A brief rest for the workers.
explanation.definitionFit: Informal word for hands, as in 'keep your paws off'.

clue.text: Old letters from the north? Sure!

indicators.note: the letters are made from the pieces rearranged

parts.note: N is the abbreviation for north

explanation.surface: Ancient writing from Scandinavia: a confident yes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'From the north' looks part of the definition, Norse script; it gives N for anagramming with SURE.
explanation.definitionFit: Characters of the old Germanic alphabets, carved in stone or wood.

clue.text: Novel by special delivery — one from SoHo, perhaps

parts.note: novel means new
a yorker is a cricket ball bowled to land at the batter's feet, a special type of delivery

explanation.surface: A book arriving by express post from a Manhattan resident.
explanation.walkthrough: SoHo here is the district of Manhattan, not London's Soho. A yorker in cricket is a ball pitched right at the batter's feet.
explanation.definitionFit: A resident of the city that contains the SoHo neighbourhood.
